corpus_definition: A unit used to measure the energy provided by food.

forms.definition: a unit for measuring how much energy food gives you
forms.example: One small apple has about 50 calories, and every calorie gives you energy.

syn.note: Energy is what your body gets from food; a calorie is the unit we use to measure it.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word. heat is connected in meaning (calorie comes from the Latin word for heat), but it is not made from calorie.

forms.definition: containing a lot of energy from food, so it can make you fat
forms.example: Fried food is very calorific, so I only eat it at weekends.
forms.note: Mainly British. American English often uses caloric.

syn.note: Everyday word for food that can make you put on weight.
Rich food has a lot of fat, sugar or cream in it.
Heavy food is hard to digest and makes you feel full.

ant.note: Light food has little fat and is easy to digest.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from this word.

context.text: My sister counts every calorie because she wants to lose weight. She says plov is too calorific, so she eats salad on weekdays.

reviewer_note: Corpus example is ungrammatical ('too many calorie counts'); our example is new. calorific kept as the adjective (in OALD/Cambridge); American caloric mentioned in a note.

corpus_definition: A person who is trying to get a job or position.

forms.definition: a person who is trying to get a job or be elected
forms.example: There are five candidates for the manager's job.

syn.note: An applicant has sent an application; candidate is also used in elections.
Someone with a real chance of winning a job, prize or competition.
A person who has been officially chosen to compete for a position or prize.

forms.definition: the fact of trying to be elected or chosen for a position
forms.example: She announced her candidacy for president of the student union.
forms.note: British English also uses candidature.
There is no verb made from this word.
There is no adjective made from this word.
There is no adverb made from this word.

context.text: Ten candidates came to the interview at the bank in Tashkent. After one candidate announced her candidacy for the top job, the others felt nervous.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6); candidacy is the state noun.

corpus_definition: The amount that can be held inside something.

forms.definition: the largest amount or number that something can hold
forms.example: The stadium has a capacity of 30,000 people.
forms.note: Also 'full to capacity' = completely full.

syn.note: Volume is the amount of space inside something, often for liquids.
Space is the empty area; capacity is how much it can hold.
Everyday word: 'Is there room for one more?'
Size is how big something is, not how much it holds.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word in this meaning.

forms.definition: having a lot of space inside
forms.example: She keeps everything in her capacious handbag.

syn.note: Everyday, informal word with the same meaning.
Common for rooms, flats and cars.
Simple general word; it does not say there is space inside.

ant.note: Without enough space for people or things.

forms.note: capaciously exists but is extremely rare; learners do not need it.

context.text: The new concert hall in Tashkent was full to capacity on Saturday. Even its capacious car park had no free spaces.

reviewer_note: Corpus example does not contain the word; new example written. Map keeps the 'amount held' sense; capable/incapacity (ability sense) left out on purpose.

corpus_definition: Things that are being moved by a ship, plane, or truck.

forms.definition: goods that a ship, plane or truck carries from place to place
forms.example: The ship carried heavy cargo across the ocean.
forms.note: Plural: cargoes or cargos.

syn.note: Very close; freight is common in business and American English.
Easy general word for things that are bought, sold or moved.
Everything one vehicle carries at one time.
One delivery of goods sent together.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word.
There is no adjective made from this word.
There is no adverb made from this word.

context.text: Every week, trains bring cargo from China to Uzbekistan. The cargo is usually clothes, phones and machines.

reviewer_note: Only one form exists; compounds like cargo ship are left out (rule 7).

corpus_definition: Being careful to avoid possible problems or dangers.

forms.definition: great care to avoid danger or mistakes
forms.example: Drive with caution when the roads are wet.

syn.note: Easy everyday word: 'Handle with care.'
Same idea, but less common.
Formal: careful and sensible thinking before acting.

ant.note: Not paying attention, so you make mistakes.
Doing dangerous things without thinking about the results.

forms.definition: something you do early to stop something bad from happening
forms.example: As a precaution, we took extra water on the trip.

forms.definition: the quality of always being careful
forms.example: His cautiousness kept him safe in the mountains.

forms.definition: to tell someone to be careful about a danger
forms.example: The guide cautioned us not to swim in the river.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
To tell someone what you think they should do.

ant.note: To tell someone to go ahead and do something.

forms.definition: careful to avoid danger or problems
forms.example: He is very cautious when walking on slippery ice.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with almost the same meaning.
Careful because you do not trust someone or something.
Formal: sensible and careful, especially with money.

ant.note: Not thinking enough about what you are doing.
Doing dangerous things without thinking.

forms.definition: in a careful way, to avoid danger or problems
forms.example: She opened the old door cautiously.

syn.note: Easy everyday word with the same meaning.
Carefully, because you do not trust something.

ant.note: Without enough attention or care.
In a dangerous way, without thinking.

context.text: My grandfather is a cautious driver. He always drives cautiously in the mountains near Chimgan, and as a precaution he checks the brakes before every trip.

reviewer_note: cautious is made from caution, so noun and verb caution are family (derivational). precaution is a common B2 word, kept as an entry (rule 2).

corpus_definition: A place where people are buried after they die.

forms.definition: an area of land where dead people are buried
forms.example: They visited the cemetery to see the graves of their grandparents.

syn.note: Same meaning; a little less formal.
Often used for very old places or places of one group of people.
The land around a church, often used for graves.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word.
There is no adjective made from this word.
There is no adverb made from this word.

context.text: Every spring, our family visits the cemetery outside the village. We clean the graves and say prayers for our grandparents.

reviewer_note: Only one form exists. Spelling trap: cemetery ends in -ery, not -ary.

corpus_definition: willing to help others and give money or time freely

forms.definition: money, food or help that is given to people in need
forms.example: They give part of their salary to charity every month.
forms.note: Also means an organization that helps people in need: 'She works for a children's charity.'

syn.note: One gift of money or things to help others.
Help, often from governments or big organizations.
The quality of being happy to give.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word.

forms.definition: happy to give money, time or help to people in need
forms.example: The charitable man donated food to the homeless shelter.
forms.note: Also means 'connected with a charity organization': a charitable trust.

syn.note: Easy everyday word: happy to give.
Informal: a giving person likes to help others.
Kind is about being nice and caring in general.
Formal: kind and wanting to help.

ant.note: Unkind or not willing to help others.
Thinking only about yourself.
British: not willing to give or spend money.

forms.definition: in a kind and generous way
forms.example: She behaved charitably towards her poor neighbours.

syn.note: Easy word with almost the same meaning.
In a nice and caring way.

ant.note: Thinking only about yourself.

context.text: My aunt is very charitable. During Ramadan she gives food to charity and helps the old people in our mahalla.

reviewer_note: charitable is made from charity; uncharitable kept as an antonym, not a form (rule 3).

corpus_definition: A quality that makes people like you.

forms.definition: a pleasant quality that makes people like you
forms.example: He used his charm to win everyone over.
forms.note: Another meaning: a small object that people think brings good luck.

syn.note: A quality that makes people interested in or like someone or something.
A feeling of liking someone, often romantically.
Your character; a strong personality is often charming.

forms.definition: to make people like you by being pleasant
forms.example: The little girl charmed all the guests at the wedding.

syn.note: To make someone very happy.
To make someone like or agree with you.
To make someone happy, not always by your personality.

ant.note: To make people dislike you or want to stay away.

forms.definition: very pleasant and easy to like
forms.example: Bukhara is a charming old city.

syn.note: Easy everyday word for something or someone very nice.
Very pleasant; a little formal.
Nice and enjoyable, but weaker.
Nice to look at; charming is more about personality.

ant.note: Not nice or enjoyable.
Not polite to other people.

forms.definition: in a very pleasant way that people like
forms.example: The old waiter smiled charmingly at the children.

syn.note: In a very pleasant way.
In a nice way, but weaker.

ant.note: In a way that is not polite.

people.definition: a person who uses pleasant ways to make others like them
people.example: Be careful, he is a real charmer.

context.text: Our new neighbour is a charming young man. He charmed my grandmother on the first day with his good manners and his charm.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the personality sense; 'lucky charm' object meaning mentioned only in a note. Compounds like charm bracelet left out.

corpus_definition: having a pattern of squares of different colors

forms.definition: a pattern of squares in different colours, on cloth
forms.example: She bought a skirt in a red and white check.
forms.note: Mainly British in this meaning. American English says plaid.

syn.note: American English for this kind of pattern, especially on clothes.
A special Scottish pattern of crossing coloured lines.

forms.definition: to look at something to see if it is correct or safe
forms.example: Please check your answers before you finish.
forms.note: Belongs to check = examine, not the square pattern on cloth.

forms.definition: having a pattern of squares in different colours
forms.example: He wore a blue checked shirt to the office.
forms.note: British English also writes chequered; American English often uses checkered or plaid.

syn.note: Having any pattern, not only squares. For squares, Americans often say plaid.

ant.note: One colour, with no pattern.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from this word.

context.text: For the school photo, Aziz wore a checked shirt. His mother said the green and white check looked nice with his dark trousers.

reviewer_note: Homograph trap: checked (pattern) vs checked (past of check = examine); verb check given as other_meaning. chequered/checkered only in a note.

corpus_definition: A substance created through a scientific process.

forms.definition: a substance that is made or used in science or industry
forms.example: Avoid touching that dangerous chemical.

syn.note: General word for any solid, liquid or gas.
In science: a substance made of two or more elements.
A simple basic substance, like oxygen or gold.

forms.note: There is no verb made from this word.

forms.definition: connected with substances and how they change and mix
forms.example: Fire is a chemical reaction.

syn.note: Made by people in a factory, not natural.
Not natural; made by people.

ant.note: Coming from nature, not made in a factory.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with substances and how they change
forms.example: The water is chemically cleaned before we drink it.

syn.note: Made by people, not in a natural way.

ant.note: In a natural way, without anything added.

people.definition: a scientist who studies substances and how they change
people.example: The chemist tested the water from the lake.
people.note: In British English a chemist is also a person who sells medicine (a pharmacist).

people.definition: the science that studies what substances are made of
people.example: My brother is studying chemistry at university in Samarkand.

context.text: Many farmers in the Fergana Valley now use fewer chemicals on their fruit. They say chemically treated apples look nice but do not taste as good.

reviewer_note: Noun and adjective share the spelling (conversion). chemist also has a British 'pharmacy' meaning, noted on the entry.
